body:
**A panel arrives with a docket claiming a date. One region of it is painted in a colour that did not exist yet. Find it.**

CRAQUELURE is a Game Boy Color game about authenticating paintings. This is the free browser demo — three lots, playable right here, no download and no account.

### The lamp is the whole game

Every painting is divided into six regions, and each region is painted in a single pigment. Under **daylight** you can only see the family: lead white, zinc white and titanium white are the same white. Natural ultramarine and French blue are the same blue. That is not the screen being limited. That is true of the actual paint.

So you change the lamp.

Under **ultraviolet** most of them come apart. Zinc white fluoresces a loud yellow-green. Titanium white goes dead black. Madder lake glows orange. Prussian blue swallows the lamp completely.

Under **raking light** you stop looking at colour and start looking at the surface. Old hand-ground mineral pigment is gritty. Bitumen tears itself into wide drying cracks. A modern machine-ground pigment is too even and barely crazes at all, and that absence is itself the tell.

Then you check the dates against the docket.

### The dates are real, and that is the point

Prussian blue 1706, cobalt 1802, chrome yellow 1809, emerald green 1814, French blue 1828, zinc white 1834, viridian 1838, cadmium yellow 1846, alizarin 1868, cadmium red 1910, titanium white 1921.

Those are the standard art-historical first-availability dates, and pigment anachronism is genuinely how forgeries get caught. It is what undid Han van Meegeren's Vermeers. So is the awkward fact that natural and synthetic ultramarine are chemically the same compound, which is why no lamp separates them and why the raking light has to exist at all.

Being straight about the rest: the dates are real and so are the best-documented ultraviolet behaviours. The remaining lamp responses are a consistent in-game forensic system, tuned so every group of look-alike pigments comes apart cleanly. This is a game about real art history. It is not a laboratory simulation and does not pretend to be one.

### Sixty-four paintings, and nobody drew any of them

Each one is composed by the cartridge's own generator: the fall of the light, the height of the table, which of five vessels stands on it, how the cloth hangs, how the fruit are heaped, whether there is a folded napkin or an open book. Every surface is computed as a lighting model and then dithered down to the two bits per pixel the hardware actually has. The craquelure is generated too, a different network on every tile, crazing according to what that region is painted with.

### Some panels are honest

Sign those off. A wrong accusation costs a strike, and so does clearing a panel that was forged. Three strikes ends the shift.

Every case was checked before it shipped: a solver that may only see what the lamps show and what the reference book says, never the answer, was run over 32,000 generated cases, and none of them was unsolvable or ambiguous.

### Controls

Left and Right choose a region. SELECT changes the lamp. B opens the reference book. A accuses. START signs the panel off as genuine.

### Honestly stated

It will not run on an original Game Boy, and that is not laziness. Colour is the evidence here: two pigments identical under daylight and different under ultraviolet are identical under both when there is no colour.

And plainly: this has never been run on physical Game Boy Color hardware. It was developed and verified against an emulator. It is a standard MBC5 image with a correct header and there is no reason to expect trouble, but we do not claim what we have not tested.

### The full cartridge

The paid version is the real 256 kB ROM you can put on a flash cart, with all sixty-four paintings as PNGs and the theme recorded off the running cartridge. It lives at https://csaf.itch.io/craquelure

Made by Core Systems Asset Factory, our sixth Game Boy cartridge and the first in colour. Tags follow.
